title: Complete measurement of tunnel- and valley-coupling parameters in a silicon double quantum dot
authors: Daniel J. King, Minyoung Kim, J. Reily, Jonathan C. Marcks, Mark Friesen, Benjamin D. Woods, M. A. Eriksson
abstract: Tunneling is essential in the initialization, measurement, and control of quantum dot qubits. In silicon, such tunneling connects not only the qubit states but also valley minima in the conduction band on opposite sides of the Brillouin zone, with large consequences for the quantum dot behavior. Here we present a full characterization of the intravalley and intervalley tunnel couplings, including their complex phases -- the valley phases. These phases are shown to control measurable parameters, including the ratios of the gaps at anticrossings between quantum states of a double quantum dot. The valley phases themselves evolve as a function of the quantum dot gate voltages and depend on the underlying atomic structure of the quantum well. Knowledge of the valley phases completes the picture and fills a key gap in our understanding of sample-wide variations of valley couplings and the physical parameters that depend on them, including spin-orbit coupling, valley-orbit mixing, and Landé $g$-factors.
summary: The paper presents a comprehensive characterization of tunnel and valley coupling parameters within a silicon double quantum dot. By employing advanced spectroscopic techniques (DAXS) and fitting data to a four-level Hamiltonian model, the authors determine complex phase factors that govern qubit behavior. This work fills a critical gap in understanding sample variations by quantifying these fundamental couplings.
main_problem: To achieve a full characterization of intravalley and intervalley tunnel couplings, including their complex phases (valley phases), in a silicon double quantum dot.
main_result: The relative strengths of the tunnel couplings are controlled by the valley phase difference ($\Delta\phi$), and incorporating the interdot-intervalley coupling ($\Delta_{RL}$) is essential for fitting experimental data accurately.
method: The study uses Detuning Axis Spectroscopy (DAXS) to measure energy dispersions, followed by fitting these measurements using a four-level Hamiltonian model derived from first principles.
model_or_system: The physical system is a Silicon/SiGe heterostructure double quantum dot (DQD). The low-energy physics is modeled by an effective four-level Hamiltonian describing electron spins and valley degrees of freedom ($\pm z$).
key_observables:
Anticrossing gaps ($E_{\mu
u}$), tunnel couplings ($	ilde{t}_{gg}, 	ilde{t}_{ee}, 	ilde{t}_{ge}, 	ilde{t}_{eg}$), and the measurable valley phases ($\Delta\phi, \Delta\phi_{RL}$).
important_parameters: Tunnel coupling magnitudes ($t_c$, $|\Delta_{RL}|$), relative valley phase differences ($\Delta\phi$), and gate voltage dependencies of these parameters.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the four-level model, which is an approximation; systematic errors are noted due to omitting higher energy orbitals.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate device structure (SEM), coupling diagrams in the valley basis, example DAXS spectra showing modulation dependence on $\Delta\phi$ and $\Delta_{RL}$, and theoretical comparisons between simulated and fitted Hamiltonian parameters.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from defining the physical problem and the four-level model to detailing the experimental measurement technique (DAXS), presenting results that show how coupling ratios depend on phases, and finally validating the method by comparing simulations against known matrix elements.
why_interesting: This work provides a detailed understanding of how subtle quantum mechanical parameters, like valley phases, govern measurable transport properties in solid-state qubits, which is crucial for designing robust quantum computing architectures.
